title: The Knights of the Right Answer
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood uses a satirical dialogue between a district Chief Comprehension Officer and a graduating student who refuses a reading comprehension test to examine what standardised tests assume about meaning. The student argues that texts do not speak and that the only shared thing is the text itself, not a single meaning. His account of students who learn to read backwards from the questions, and of a teacher who taught the passage and questions as one unified text, shows how test-taking skills can diverge from comprehension. Underwood then moves to the NAEP reading framework revision, where constructivist and sociocultural proposals on prior knowledge were resisted by Chester Finn and others in favour of a decontextualised model of reading. His claim is that tests guarded by the Knights of the Right Answer measure a narrow desert-island reading rather than how people comprehend in context. The form is fiction, but the argument about assessment design and comprehension theory is explicit.
points: Treating comprehension as retrieving the one right meaning from the four corners of the text ignores that readers construct meaning.
Students can pass comprehension tests by reading backwards from the questions and learn nothing, so test success is a weak proxy for understanding.
Teaching students to critique the passage, questions and distractors as one text turns test-taking into genuine analysis.
Current reading theory holds that assessment must account for prior knowledge, yet the 2026 NAEP framework resisted that shift under pressure from Finn and allies.
Finn's own admission that he could work out an unfamiliar word with effort but that test takers cannot look it up exposes how artificial test conditions are.
quotes: My test doesn’t ask you what you think the text means,” Mr. Bubbles, the Chief Comprehension Officer for the district, said. “It asks you what the text means.
Texts don’t say anything,” Phaedrus replied. “People say things when they speak. Texts are silent. If they spoke, they would not be texts.
She became an expert in reading backwards, passed all the comprehension tests, and learned nothing. She got As.

Teacher explained how two texts make one, that, together, the passage and the questions formed a unified text. They implicated one another. Each part could be read alone, but the two-part design was made to function as a single system.

Understanding of the role of prior knowledge in comprehension had enlarged—instead of simply acknowledging the role, current theory of comprehension held that assessment must account for its consequences. How a reader adjusts cognition to maximize and monitor prior knowledge is integral to comprehension as a process.
This reader, Mr. Finn, is aware that comprehension is an active process requiring motivation. He can monitor his progress and make executive decisions: “Possibly I could look that one up,” he writes.

As Chief Comprehension Officer for his district, Mr. Bubbles experienced a degree of disequilibrium. He felt sad that the 2026 NAEP test would be designed without the benefit of scientific research over the past twenty years.
